articles.title: LX Pantos expands US presence with new Chicago office

articles.body: LX Pantos Americas has opened a new office in the Chicago area, strengthening its presence in the US Midwest as part of its regional expansion strategy. The company marked the opening with a ribbon-cutting ceremony on 12 November 2026 in Rolling Meadows, Illinois. The event brought together customers, business partners and representatives of the local logistics community. The new office will support LX Pantos’ customer relationships and business development activities across the Midwest, an important market for manufacturing, distribution and international freight. Chicago’s established air, rail, road and intermodal connections also provide access to major domestic and international supply chains. Chicago office supports regional logistics operations The new location complements LX Pantos Americas’ existing operations in Illinois, where the company has approximately 900,000 square feet of warehouse capacity. LX Pantos provides a range of logistics services across the Americas, including ocean freight, air freight, ground transportation, warehousing and supply chain management. The Chicago office will serve as an additional centre for customer engagement and regional business development. “LX Pantos has long recognized the strategic importance of the Midwest,” said David Bang, CEO, LX Pantos Americas. “The opening of our Chicago office reflects our continued commitment to being closer to our customers, investing in regions that drive economic growth and creating new opportunities to support businesses navigating increasingly complex supply chains,” Bang added. The expansion follows the opening of LX Pantos Americas’ regional headquarters in Teaneck, New Jersey, earlier this year. Headquartered in South Korea, LX Pantos operates an international logistics network spanning more than 40 countries. The company has not disclosed the investment associated with the Chicago office or the number of employees based at the new location.

articles.title: Sea-Intelligence: NAWC Import Growth at 17.6% in September
articles.summary: In 2026‑Q3, North America West Coast (NAWC) ports experienced steady overall volume growth, driven almost entirely by a 17.6% Y/Y surge in laden imports in September. articles.body: In 2026‑Q3, North America West Coast (NAWC) ports experienced steady overall volume growth, driven almost entirely by a 17.6% Y/Y surge in laden imports in September. Following a sluggish start to the quarter, where laden imports contracted by ‑3.9% Y/Y in July and stabilized in August, September volumes surged to 1.45 million TEU. This double‑digit percentage growth in September is partially exaggerated by an unusually weak 2025‑Q3 baseline, when laden import growth dropped by ‑12.5 percentage points between July and September 2025. Still, 2026 marks the highest September laden import volume on record for the West Coast, eclipsing the previous high set in 2024. Overall, for 2026-Q3, NAWC ports recorded a 2.6% Y/Y increase in total container volume throughput, bringing the aggregate volume to 8.32 million TEU for the quarter. This growth was heavily weighted towards inbound cargo, with laden imports growing by 3.9% to reach 4.12 million TEU. In contrast, outbound cargo experienced more muted growth, as laden exports increased by just 1.8% to 1.21 million TEU, and empty container exports saw a smaller increase of 1.1% Y/Y to 2.67 million TEU. The operational impact of this highly compressed peak season has been substantial. Rather than managing a smoothed‑out influx of seasonal cargo, terminals were forced to handle an 11.3% M/M jump in laden imports from August to September, which is the highest M/M September increase across the 2012 to 2026 period. This level of sudden volatility creates acute stress on port infrastructure, chassis availability, and rail networks. As shippers navigated this, they overwhelmingly prioritized the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, which captured 73% of the West Coast’s total laden imports in 2026‑Q3.

articles.title: Middle East Conflict Could Cut Global Oil Demand by 4%
articles.summary: The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response…
articles.body: Middle East Conflict Could Cut Global Oil Demand by 4% Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 19, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Yellow Boat The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday. Energy markets have been rattled this year by the conflict, which has curbed shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a route that typically carries about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies and is a key artery for Gulf exports. "In my view, the energy world will never be the same again as it was before the Iran war," IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said in an interview alongside the release of the agency's World Energy Outlook 2026. The conflict has resulted in cumulative losses of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas supplies from the Gulf, the Paris-based agency said. The annual outlook includes a range of scenarios based on existing and proposed energy policies. This year it also examines how governments and markets could respond to prolonged disruption in Hormuz. Under a new Additional Response Case (ARC), the IEA said energy security concerns could speed up electrification, energy-efficiency measures and efforts to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels. In that case, global oil demand in 2035 is 4.4 million barrels per day lower than under the agency's Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), which reflects governments' current policy intentions. Electric vehicles alone would displace more than 11 million bpd of oil demand. Global oil demand falls to 97 million bpd in 2035 and 85 million bpd by 2050 under ARC, compared with just over 101 million bpd in 2035 under STEPS. Gas demand under ARC is more than 300 bcm lower than under STEPS. ELECTRIFICATION GROWING The report said electrification is now cost-competitive across large parts of transport, heating and industry, although inadequate grids, charging networks and power supplies could slow its rollout. "Many countries are seeing electrification as a policy option for energy security. Instead of importing energy, they decided to build energy at home," Birol said. Electricity's share of final energy consumption is projected to approach 30% globally under STEPS, up from about 23% today, as transport, heating and parts of industry switch away from fossil fuels. Alongside data centres, rising demand for cooling is emerging as one of the strongest drivers of electricity consumption. For the first time, demand for cooling in buildings has exceeded demand for heating, the IEA said, as higher temperatures and rising incomes drive rapid growth in air-conditioner use. articles.title: Constanta Port Grain Exports Rise by Double Digits in 2026
articles.summary: Grain exports through Romania's Black Sea port of Constanta rose by double digits in the first 10 months of the year, the port authority said, helped by a good harvest, strong demand and Ukrainian exports passing through the port.The Constanta…
articles.body: Constanta Port Grain Exports Rise by Double Digits in 2026 Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 19, 2026 © Adobe Stock/dudlajzov Grain exports through Romania's Black Sea port of Constanta rose by double digits in the first 10 months of the year, the port authority said, helped by a good harvest, strong demand and Ukrainian exports passing through the port. The Constanta port authority told Reuters the total volume of goods shipped through the port by end-October stood at 59.0 million tons, up 3.5% on the year. Grain exports through the port, one of the largest in the European Union, totaled 18.5 million tons, up 17.1% on the year. Ukrainian grain exports through Constanta jumped to 1.65 million tons compared with 321,000 tons in the first 10 months of 2025 as Kyiv sought alternative routes due to Russian attacks on its own seaports. The near five-year war between Russia and Ukraine has spilled over into the Black Sea, with some 15 merchant vessels hit over the past six weeks off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria. Romania has said it is a target of Russia's hybrid war, which Moscow has repeatedly denied. The escalating maritime war off the coasts of European Union and NATO members Romania and Bulgaria is creating a major challenge for NATO, intelligence experts have said. The strikes focused mainly on ships headed to and from Romania's Sulina Canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea and is the primary export route for Ukraine, one of the world's largest grain exporters. Constanta has not been targeted despite the recent attacks. The port data does not include volumes handled through smaller Romanian ports and direct exports by rail and road. Romania is one of the EU's biggest grain exporters and Constanta also handles flows from landlocked neighbours including Serbia, Hungary and Moldova. To reflect rising Black Sea grain trade, Euronext said earlier this month it will launch Black Sea wheat and corn futures next year with physical delivery to the port of Constanta. "From an operational perspective Constanta does not have a problem; the grain terminals are moving well," Cezar Gheorghe of Romanian grain market consultancy AGRIColumn told Reuters. Gheorghe, who worked with Euronext to set up the futures service, said logistics costs had increased because of higher fuel prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East, as well as railroad bottlenecks because of Romanian infrastructure works and a shortage of locomotives. He said a good harvest in Romania, strong demand and relatively good sea transport costs for Constanta helped boost exports. (Reuters)

articles.title: StormGeo weather intelligence strengthens climate resilience for Brazilian state with Climatempo’s Radar RS project
articles.summary: The new Radar RS project implemented by StormGeo subsidiary Climatempo in the Brazilian State of Rio Grande do Sul is integrating advanced radar technology with weather intelligence to turn atmospheric data into improved decision-making to safeguard lives and infrastructure. “Timely data about developing weather...
articles.body: StormGeo weather intelligence strengthens climate resilience for Brazilian state with Climatempo’s Radar RS project in International Shipping News 19/11/2026 The new Radar RS project implemented by StormGeo subsidiary Climatempo in the Brazilian State of Rio Grande do Sul is integrating advanced radar technology with weather intelligence to turn atmospheric data into improved decision-making to safeguard lives and infrastructure. “Timely data about developing weather systems combined with actionable insights are becoming increasingly important to provide authorities and stakeholders with real-time intelligence to more effectively respond to severe weather,” said Climatempo’s CEO, Patricia Diehl Madeira. “Installation of the radar infrastructure is the starting point. Weather intelligence goes beyond the forecast – its value lies in converting complex meteorological data from multiple sources into information to support critical decisions amid rapidly changing conditions.” StormGeo’s CEO Kim Sørensen. Photo: StormGeo Enhancing monitoring capabilities The Radar RS weather monitoring and intelligence system is designed to enhance monitoring capabilities, and bolster emergency preparedness and response to protect citizens from extreme weather and flooding in one of Brazil’s most climate-vulnerable regions. In 2024, Rio Grande do Sul experienced severe flooding that affected hundreds of municipalities, displaced hundreds of thousands of people, and caused significant loss of life and damage to infrastructure. As extreme weather events become more frequent and intense, the state is strengthening its meteorological monitoring and response capabilities to reduce risk, protect communities and build long‑term climate resilience. Climatempo, a wholly-owned unit of StormGeo, is combining its local meteorological expertise with radar technology under the flagship project that comprises three S-band weather radars, data integration, and specialised meteorological and geological monitoring. Radar deployment entailed significant technical analysis of terrain, obstacles, access, safety, power, connectivity, radio-frequency interference, beam blockage and radar coverage to ensure optimal site selection. Nine sites were ranked as the highest-scoring locations – out of 32 coordinates initially studied – and organised into three geographic regions to support design of a three-radar network. Climatempo’s CEO Patricia Diehl Madeira. Photo: StormGeo Integrated radar solution The system integrates radar observations with satellites, lightning data, weather stations and meteorological models to provide a broader basis for analysis and interpretation. Integrated data can support real-time visualisation, storm-evolution tracking and very-short-range forecasting, helping to provide more context for monitoring and alerts. Climatempo’s team of meteorologists and data specialists use this integrated picture to provide continuous monitoring and operational decision support to the state’s civil defence and emergency management teams. Atmospheric signals can be turned into information to interpret weather, track its evolution, support alerts, and strengthen preparation and response to heavy rain, storms, strong winds and other extreme events. This can improve early warnings, emergency response and climate resilience for millions of residents in areas at risk. From observation to anticipation “When severe weather is developing, knowing that a storm exists is only the beginning. The real challenge is understanding where it is moving, how it is evolving and what that could mean for people and infrastructure,” said Diehl Madeira. “The objective is not to create more weather data, but to create a more complete and usable picture of the atmosphere. Meteorological intelligence is key to understanding, integrating and interpreting weather information so that it can support decisions. “The real value comes from combining high-quality observations with meteorological expertise, data integration, modelling and interpretation to provide decision-makers with a clearer picture of what is happening and what may happen next.” A sophisticated weather-intelligence system provides faster access to information but still requires meteorological expertise to understand atmospheric behaviour, uncertainty and the evolution of weather systems, she underlined. The S-band radar shown during acceptance testing in August 2026 at a site in Rio Grande do Sul. Photo: Climatempo Mitigation of climate risk By combining robust infrastructure with local meteorological intelligence, the Radar RS system is expected to improve the accuracy and lead time of severe‑weather alerts, giving authorities more time to organise evacuations, protect critical assets and coordinate emergency response. Over time, the state aims to reduce the human, social and economic costs of flooding and other extreme events, while sharing learnings that can benefit other regions facing similar climate risks. The Radar RS project illustrates a broader shift in the role of weather information as continuous observation, multiple data sources, sophisticated interpretation, decision-support tools and integration into operational workflows become necessary to manage increasingly complex weather risks, with application across multiple sectors. “Weather is not simply something organisations need to know about; it is an operational input that can influence decisions,” said StormGeo’s CEO, Kim Sørensen. “Around the world, we see a growing need for integrated weather‑intelligence solutions that turn complex data into clear, actionable guidance. Radar RS demonstrates how our group, through Climatempo, can partner with public authorities to build solutions that can be replicated in other countries facing similar climate risks.” Source: StormGeo 2026-11-19 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Crew Welfare Day at IMPA Singapore to explore the human side of procurement
articles.summary: Decisions made ashore about which goods and services to buy can affect seafarers’ safety, wellbeing and access to support at sea. articles.body: Crew Welfare Day at IMPA Singapore to explore the human side of procurement in International Shipping News 19/11/2026 Decisions made ashore about which goods and services to buy can affect seafarers’ safety, wellbeing and access to support at sea. The Nautical Institute will examine that link at Crew Welfare Day at IMPA Singapore on Tuesday 24 November. As ships become more connected and automated, the programme will consider how procurement teams can take crews’ needs into account when new technology is introduced on board. The event brings together procurement professionals, technology providers and welfare advocates under the theme ‘Transforming Maritime Together: Procurement, Innovation & the Human Experience’. The opening session, ‘From cost centres to human outcomes: Redefining maritime procurement’, will look at what procurement teams can take into account when weighing costs, including how the goods and services they procure can support crew welfare and education. ‘Smart procurement, smarter welfare? AI, data, and the human reality at sea’ will examine how artificial intelligence and data can inform procurement decisions. The question for shore teams is how those tools can help them account for the needs of the seafarers who rely on the goods and services they buy. The discussion then turns to ‘Connected ships, connected decisions: Digital supply chains that serve people’. The session will consider how digital links between ship and shore affect what crews can access on board, from supplies to training. The final session, ‘High-tech ships, high-risk blind spots: Welfare and training in the age of automation’, will look at the opportunities and risks of increasing automation. It will consider how greater use of autonomous systems could affect crew welfare and what training seafarers need as their work changes. articles.body: ReCAAP Information Sharing Centre Conducts Cluster Meeting in Myanmar in International Shipping News 19/11/2026 The ReCAAP Information Sharing Centre (ISC) and the Myanmar Focal Point today concluded a four-day Cluster Meeting held from 16 to 19 November 2026 in Yangon, Myanmar. The meeting brought together representatives from the Myanmar Navy, Myanmar Coast Guard, Myanmar Department of Marine Administration and Myanma Port Authority to discuss maritime security concerns and ways to strengthen inter-agency coordination in addressing armed robbery against ships in ports, anchorages and territorial waters. The meeting was attended by officers from ReCAAP Focal Points in Bangladesh, India and Thailand, as well as representatives from the Indonesia Marine and Air Police Corps (IMAP) and the Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency (MMEA). The meeting provided a platform for participants to exchange experiences, share operational insights and discuss common maritime security challenges. Presentations covered a range of key topics, including: • Challenges in maritime governance and monitoring illicit activities at sea; • Strengthening ship and port security through the implementation of the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code; • Information sharing and international cooperation in combating transnational maritime crimes; and • Best practices for timely and accurate incident reporting by shipping companies. Participants also engaged in group discussions on two key topics: “Enhancing Engagement and Cooperation between the Shipping Industry and Maritime Agencies” and “Emerging Maritime Security Challenges in the Bay of Bengal”. The discussions focused on strengthening communication and coordination among maritime stakeholders, improving information sharing and identifying opportunities for enhanced regional cooperation in addressing evolving maritime security threats. Participants of ReCAAP ISC Cluster Meeting held from 16 to 19 November 2026 ReCAAP ISC Executive Director, Mr Vijay D. Chafekar, said: “The littoral states of the Bay of Bengal and the Gulf of Thailand face a range of transnational maritime security threats, including sea robbery, illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing, drug trafficking and irregular migration by sea. This Cluster Meeting has provided a valuable opportunity for Myanmar and neighbouring ReCAAP Focal Points to exchange perspectives on shared sub-regional maritime security concerns and explore ways to strengthen inter-state cooperation and mutual trust in addressing transnational maritime crimes particularly piracy & armed robbery incidents. Continued information sharing, mutual trust and close collaboration among maritime agencies are essential to ensuring a coordinated response to these challenges.” Commander Han Tun Aung, Commanding Officer (1st Fleet), Myanmar Navy and ReCAAP ISC Governor for Myanmar, said: “Over the past two decades, ReCAAP ISC has played an important role in strengthening regional cooperation to combat piracy and armed robbery against ships in Asia through the sharing of verified incident reports, information and analytical insights with ReCAAP Focal Points. The Myanmar Navy and Myanmar Coast Guard remain committed to supporting the Centre’s capacity-building initiatives and strengthening cooperation with regional maritime partners to help keep regional waters safe and secure for seafarers and maritime trade.” The Cluster Meeting reaffirmed the importance of sustained engagement, timely and accurate incident reporting, effective information sharing and stronger partnerships among maritime agencies and the shipping industry. It also underscored the value of the ReCAAP framework as a platform for promoting regional cooperation and collective efforts to address piracy, armed robbery against ships and other emerging maritime security challenges in Asia. articles.body: KONGSBERG joins Brave Prime to strengthen collaboration with Ukrainian industry in International Shipping News 19/11/2026 KONGSBERG signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Brave1 in Kyiv, making it the third foreign defence company to join the Brave Prime initiative. The partnership aims to combine KONGSBERG’s global industrial and defence expertise with the speed, agility and frontline feedback of Ukrainian innovators. The partnership will explore KONGSBERG’s technology and solutions, relevant to Ukraine’s current defence needs, as well as provide testing opportunities for the company’s solutions through Brave1’s ‘Test in Ukraine’ framework. Brave Prime also facilitates matchmaking with domestic defence technology companies to explore integration of Ukrainian technologies and components. The initiative also aims to identify areas for joint research and development. “The future of European defence will be built through stronger connections between global industrial capabilities and the innovation happening in Ukraine,” said Iryna Zabolotna, Chief Operating Officer of Brave1. “With KONGSBERG joining Brave Prime, we are taking another step toward building lasting industrial relationships with the world’s leading defence companies and creating new opportunities for joint development and production”. “Joining Brave Prime opens up for even deeper collaboration between KONGSBERG and Ukrainian industry and authorities and can be an enabler for faster innovation to benefit Ukraine and Europe,” said Aslak Sverdrup, head of KONGSBERG in Ukraine. “We are proud to support Ukraine and to be working closely with the Ukrainians, and we look forward to further cooperation as part of the Brave1 framework.” Brave Prime was launched by the Ukrainian government-backed defence tech cluster Brave1 in June 2026 with the aim of bringing leading global defence companies into Ukraine’s defence-tech ecosystem and creating opportunities for deeper product-level cooperation. KONGSBERG’s technology and solutions, including the NASAMS air defence system, has operated in Ukraine since 2022, helping to protect people and critical infrastructure against aerial threats such as drones, cruise missiles and aircraft. In contrast, the services surplus widened to €23.7 billion from €16.3 billion, while the primary income surplus increased to €3.5 billion from almost zero. Meanwhile, the secondary income deficit remained broadly stable at €15.9 billion, compared with €15.5 billion in September 2025. For the first nine months of 2026, the cumulative current account surplus declined to €160.0 billion, from €180.8 billion in the same period of 2025. articles.title: Iran Intensifies Hormuz Tanker Attacks Just as Oil Prices Slide
articles.summary: Iran’s attacks on oil tankers crossing the crucial Strait of Hormuz are getting more intense, just as prices have tumbled due to a flood of supply from the Middle East.

(Screenshot from video) (Bloomberg) — Iran’s attacks on oil tankers crossing the crucial Strait of Hormuz are getting more intense, just as prices have tumbled due to a flood of supply from the Middle East. After a period of low-grade clashes, attacks increased in October and continued at the higher tempo this month, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. In a sign of the mounting severity, at least two seafarers are missing after attacks this week. Traders and shipowners also circulated videos of a vessel engulfed in flames this week, though Bloomberg couldn’t immediately verify the footage. The flareups are happening as Brent crude futures slid about a fifth this month as Middle East exports approached pre-war levels, with the International Energy Agency last week saying that supply is outpacing demand for the first time since the war began. However, flows appear to have pulled back recently, though it’s not clear whether that’s due to intensifying attacks, with shipments often volatile from week to week and month to month. Critically, it’s also hard to quickly gauge how badly vessels are being hit as producers tend to remain tight-lipped due to security concerns. A key question is whether the attacks will be enough to meaningfully impact oil supply. “It seems like the new normal: Something like a war, but not exactly a war, with attacks on ships virtually every day,” said Georgios Sakellariou, an analyst at shipping-analytics platform Signal Ocean. “Oil is going out, but being certain about the volumes is complicated by the attacks and the secrecy.” Another issue is that while oil is flowing through Hormuz, more and more vessels will be needed as some are lost to attacks, he said. There are signs that attacks are becoming more serious. Several maritime security officials have said that Iran has attempted to hit the same ship on multiple occasions to deter salvors, and that there have also been sightings of limpet mines attached to vessels. One Gulf oil official said the situation in and around Hormuz had deteriorated since the US midterms. Gulf producers rely on energy exports to fund their economies. One senior Saudi shipping official said at a conference last week that the kingdom has no choice but to continue shipping oil through Hormuz, despite the attacks. Traders, analysts and shipping officials generally collate data from UK Maritime Trade Operations and the International Maritime Organization to assess the severity of attacks. But Gulf producers rarely release public information about attacks to help protect the security of vessels. So far this month, UKMTO has reported roughly one attack a day, with about 14 incidents occurring in Hormuz. Last month, it said it was struggling to accurately report the number of attacks as many companies weren’t reporting incidents to authorities. That’s fueling uncertainty about exactly how many attacks there are, as well as rampant rumors and speculation on vessels within commodity trading circles. While there’s also uncertainty about flows through Hormuz, there are signs that they have fallen from elevated levels this month, according to data from intelligence firms Kpler and Vortexa. The seven-day moving average of oil transits through Hormuz and net ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman eased to about 10 million barrels a day by Nov. 10, from around 13.4 million at the start of the month, Kpler data show. Recent data remain provisional as additional vessel crossings continue to be identified and validated. As producers boosted output last month, Saudi Arabia told the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries that the amount it actually supplied to the market was below its production. In the past, such a discrepancy has been an indication the kingdom was filling storage tanks or getting more out of Hormuz in advance of any escalation in the war. Both sides have lately stepped up tit-for-tat attacks in the ongoing war. US warplanes hit an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Persian Gulf this week, a response to Iran earlier targeting US personnel and assets. The chances of the US launching another round of mass strikes against Iran appear to have grown in recent days, according to Western officials, and the US issued a fresh warning to vessels breaching its blockade of Iranian ports this week. While the oil market has largely taken the recent flareups in its stride, that could change if attacks worsen. Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. said this week that one of its ships was hit when crossing Hormuz, that one seafarer was unaccounted for and a further 11 were injured. Kuwait has written to the IMO about attacks on eight of its tankers in recent weeks too. “Such actions undermine the security and stability of the region and constitute a clear breach of international law,” it said in a letter this week. “Kuwait reiterates its demands that the Islamic Republic of Iran immediately cease its unlawful attacks.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: Panama's comptroller general said on Wednesday it had filed a criminal complaint over suspected irregularities uncovered in an audit of a state contract with a unit of Hong Kong conglomerate CK Hutchison.

REUTERS/Enea Lebrun PANAMA CITY, Nov 18 (Reuters) – Panama’s comptroller general said on Wednesday it had filed a criminal complaint over suspected irregularities uncovered in an audit of a state contract with a unit of Hong Kong conglomerate CK Hutchison . The comptroller’s office said the complaint seeks an investigation into possible crimes linked to the port concession contract between the state and the CK Hutchison unit, Panama Ports Company (PPC). It said the filing covers former board members of the Panama Maritime Authority between 2014 and 2023, former administrators of the authority during that period, and PPC itself. The authority and PPC did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The complaint stems from findings in an audit of the company’s financial statements and compliance with contractual obligations, the comptroller said. The office did not detail the suspected irregularities, but said it had turned over documentation to the public prosecutor for investigation. The move marks the latest development in a broader dispute over PPC’s role operating the Balboa and Cristobal ports near the Panama Canal, one of the world’s busiest maritime waterways. Earlier this year, Panama moved to unwind the company’s port concessions, escalating a legal and diplomatic fight involving PPC and CK Hutchison. PPC has also accused Panamanian authorities in recent months of unlawfully seizing property and documents during the takeover of the facilities, allegations President Jose Raul Mulino has rejected. The dispute has complicated CK Hutchison’s proposed sale of a majority stake in its global ports business to a consortium led by BlackRock and Mediterranean Shipping Company. articles.title: Climatempo Integrates Radar Technology, Weather Intelligence to Bolster Storm Resilience
articles.summary: The new Radar RS project implemented by StormGeo subsidiary Climatempo in the Brazilian State of Rio Grande do Sul is integrating radar technology with weather intelligence to turn atmospheric data into improved decision-making to safeguard lives and infrastructure.In 2024…
articles.body: Climatempo Integrates Radar Technology, Weather Intelligence to Bolster Storm Resilience Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 19, 2026 The S-band radar shown during acceptance testing in August 2026 at a site in Rio Grande do Sul. Photo: Climatempo The new Radar RS project implemented by StormGeo subsidiary Climatempo in the Brazilian State of Rio Grande do Sul is integrating radar technology with weather intelligence to turn atmospheric data into improved decision-making to safeguard lives and infrastructure. In 2024, Rio Grande do Sul experienced severe flooding that affected hundreds of municipalities, displaced hundreds of thousands of people, and caused significant loss of life and damage to infrastructure. As extreme weather events become more frequent and intense, the state is strengthening its meteorological monitoring and response capabilities to reduce risk, protect communities and build long‑term climate resilience. The Radar RS weather monitoring and intelligence system is designed to enhance monitoring capabilities and bolster emergency preparedness and response to protect citizens from extreme weather and flooding in one of Brazil’s most climate-vulnerable regions. Climatempo, a wholly-owned unit of StormGeo, is combining its local meteorological expertise with radar technology under the flagship project that comprises three S-band weather radars, data integration, and specialized meteorological and geological monitoring. Radar deployment entailed significant technical analysis of terrain, obstacles, access, safety, power, connectivity, radio-frequency interference, beam blockage and radar coverage to ensure optimal site selection. Nine sites were ranked as the highest-scoring locations – out of 32 coordinates initially studied – and organized into three geographic regions to support design of a three-radar network. Integrated radar solution The system integrates radar observations with satellites, lightning data, weather stations and meteorological models to provide a broader basis for analysis and interpretation. Integrated data can support real-time visualiation, storm-evolution tracking and very-short-range forecasting, helping to provide more context for monitoring and alerts. Climatempo’s team of meteorologists and data specialists use this integrated picture to provide continuous monitoring and operational decision support to the state’s civil defense and emergency management teams. Atmospheric signals can be turned into information to interpret weather, track its evolution, support alerts, and strengthen preparation and response to heavy rain, storms, strong winds and other extreme events. This can improve early warnings, emergency response and climate resilience for millions of residents in areas at risk. Mitigation of climate risk By combining robust infrastructure with local meteorological intelligence, the Radar RS system is expected to improve the accuracy and lead time of severe‑weather alerts, giving authorities more time to organize evacuations, protect critical assets and coordinate emergency response. Over time, the state aims to reduce the human, social and economic costs of flooding and other extreme events, while sharing learnings that can benefit other regions facing similar climate risks. The Radar RS project illustrates a broader shift in the role of weather information as continuous observation, multiple data sources, sophisticated interpretation, decision-support tools and integration into operational workflows become necessary to manage increasingly complex weather risks, with application across multiple sectors.

Photo: Hanwha Philly Shipyard Hanwha Philly Shipyard has begun construction of the first of four medium-range (MR) oil and chemical tankers for Hanwha Shipping, marking the start of a new U.S.-built tanker program as the South Korean conglomerate expands its American shipbuilding operations. The Philadelphia shipyard held a steel-cutting ceremony on November 17, kicking off a multiyear construction program with vessel deliveries scheduled between 2029 and 2030. The four tankers, each approximately 49,500 deadweight tons, will be designed to transport crude oil, refined petroleum products and chemicals. The vessels will be built to comply with the Jones Act, which requires vessels carrying cargo between U.S. ports to be American-built, American-owned and American-crewed. According to Hanwha Philly Shipyard , the tankers will feature energy-efficient designs and meet International Maritime Organization Type 2 and Type 3 chemical tanker standards. An optional Type II configuration with 18 segregations will allow the vessels to carry different cargoes separately. The program represents the first construction of an MR tanker in the United States in nearly a decade, according to Hanwha Shipping. “At a time when the domestic tanker fleet continues to age, these vessels will help modernize U.S. maritime transportation and enhance the resilience of America’s energy supply chain,” said James Sagar, CEO of Hanwha Shipping. (Image: UK Marine Accident Investigation Branch) British marine accident investigators are calling for changes to superyacht safety regulations after the sinking of the luxury sailing yacht Bayesian exposed gaps in vessel stability standards, liferaft requirements and crew training that could put other large sailing yachts at risk. The recommendations, contained in the UK Marine Accident Investigation Branch’s (MAIB) final report released Thursday , follow the August 2024 disaster off Sicily that killed seven people, including British technology entrepreneur Mike Lynch and his daughter. While investigators found that Bayesian had an unrecognized vulnerability to extreme winds , the report goes further, identifying shortcomings in the regulatory framework governing large sailing yachts and recommending changes aimed at preventing similar accidents. At the center of the findings is a gap in the standards used to assess yacht stability. Neither the Large Commercial Yacht Code (LY2), under which Bayesian was built, nor the subsequent Red Ensign Group Yacht Code required certain monohull sailing yachts to be assessed for the risk of being knocked onto their sides by high winds when operating without sails. Investigators found that the yacht’s towering mast and furled sails still generated substantial wind forces, even while the vessel was anchored. However, its approved stability information did not account for that risk, leaving the crew unaware of a potentially catastrophic vulnerability. The MAIB has recommended that the Red Ensign Group study the vulnerability of monohull sailing yachts certified under its Yacht Code and amend the regulations based on its findings. It also wants improved stability information and operational guidance for crews preparing for extreme weather, whether underway or at anchor. The investigation identified another significant safety concern involving lifesaving equipment. None of Bayesian ‘s liferafts automatically floated free and inflated when the yacht sank. Although their hydrostatic release units operated, the rafts remained trapped by their stowage arrangements. A crew member was forced to manually release one, allowing the 15 survivors to remain afloat until they were rescued. Investigators found that the liferaft arrangements met the regulatory requirements applicable when the yacht was originally surveyed. However, those standards did not adequately address what happens when a large sailing yacht is knocked onto its side. The MAIB is now recommending amendments to the Red Ensign Group Yacht Code requiring liferafts aboard sailing vessels vulnerable to knockdown to be capable of floating free, inflating and separating from the vessel as it sinks. The report also identified a separate deficiency in Bayesian ‘s original stability approval. Investigators determined that the yacht did not meet LY2’s minimum downflooding-angle requirement, leaving it vulnerable to progressive flooding at lower heel angles than the code permitted. The MAIB classified that finding as a safety issue that did not directly contribute to the accident. Beyond vessel design, investigators are calling for improvements in marine weather forecasting and professional training. Thunderstorms had been forecast near the yacht’s anchorage, but the available warnings did not adequately communicate the potential for destructive downbursts. Within just 14 minutes, relatively calm conditions gave way to winds of at least 68 knots, knocking the yacht onto its side in less than 15 seconds. The MAIB has recommended that the UK’s Maritime and Coastguard Agency review yacht officer training requirements to better address thunderstorms, downbursts and extreme wind gusts. It has also urged the Met Office to raise the treatment of rare but potentially catastrophic weather events with the World Meteorological Organization, while calling for updated guidance in Admiralty nautical publications. In a separate safety flyer issued to the yachting industry , the MAIB urged yacht owners, managers and crews to examine their vessels’ vulnerability to extreme weather and ensure their operating procedures adequately address the risks. “Our investigation found that Bayesian had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised,” said Rob Loder, the UK’s Chief Inspector of Marine Accidents. Loder urged regulators, training providers and weather services to act on the investigation’s recommendations to prevent another tragedy. The proposed changes are not yet binding regulations. According to the final report, no safety actions had been taken by other organizations at the time of publication. The MAIB has also prepared a paper detailing the hazards identified in the investigation for consideration by the International Maritime Organization’s Sub-Committee on Implementation of IMO Instruments, potentially extending the safety discussion beyond the superyacht sector. articles.title: Crawling to the Rescue: Tiny Robots Built to Inspect Nuclear Waste Pipes
articles.summary: How do you inspect underground pipes that carry contaminated waste from the inside out? It’s a question the Hanford Site in Washington state has faced as it works to clean up the waste left by decades of nuclear production. With no easy solution…
articles.body: Crawling to the Rescue: Tiny Robots Built to Inspect Nuclear Waste Pipes Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 19, 2026 The robotics team at Sandia National Laboratories has built the SPIINE robot to inspect small pipes at the Department of Energy’s Hanford Site. Armed with LED lights, an onboard camera and a flexible body, it can easily drive through 90-degree turns and document its environment. (Photo by Craig Fritz) The robotics team at Sandia National Laboratories shows off an updated version of the SPIINE pipe crawler, designed to maneuver through and help inspect 2-inch pipes at the Hanford Site in Washington state. (Photo by Craig Fritz) How do you inspect underground pipes that carry contaminated waste from the inside out? It’s a question the Hanford Site in Washington state has faced as it works to clean up the waste left by decades of nuclear production. With no easy solution, Hanford turned to the Sandia National Laboratories and their tiny robot, who have come to the rescue. The Hanford Site pipe network Hanford is a decommissioned nuclear production complex managed by the Department of Energy. Located on the Columbia River, it was established in 1943 as part of the Manhattan Project and housed the world’s first full-scale plutonium production reactor. The Plutonium produced at the site was used in the first atomic bomb. What’s left at Hanford is radioactive waste that is housed in underground storage tanks, connected by a network of pipes. These pipes are designed to transfer waste from one tank to another, but the pipes are decades old and must be inspected to ensure they are in good condition. The pipes are hard to access–they're underground, run hundreds of feet in various directions, are double-walled and measure as little as two inches in diameter. Digging up these pipes for a visual inspection isn’t realistic or cost-effective. It also can’t ensure that pipes aren’t corroding from the inside out. While sending tiny cameras inside the pipes might seem like the obvious solution, earlier attempts had limited success. Traditional “push” cameras used for visual inspection could travel only about 10 feet at a time and were unable to maneuver tight 90-degree bends. The team also tried volumetric inspections using ultrasound, but the conventional probes are often too bulky to navigate through smaller pipes with tight bends. Tiny solution A Sandia team led by mechanical engineer Steve Buerger believes the solution is a tiny robot designed to propel itself through the pipes. “When we saw this need, we thought this is an area we can leverage some of those past works, do something unique, and really help with a very big problem,” Buerger said. “Sandia has made a lot of strides in making systems that are very small but still large enough to do real physical work.” Buerger and his team, which includes Daniel McArthur, Derya Tansel, Clint Hobart, and Josh Ortiz, came up with a robot called SPIINE, which stands for Self-Propelled Interior Inspector for Non-destructive-testing Examination. The robot is tiny in stature, measuring only two inches by six inches, but mighty in its abilities. It has a multi-axis body, adaptive wheels, steering capabilities and a high-resolution camera with adjustable LED lighting. Its motors are powerful enough to not only transport itself but carry a payload, such as an ultrasonic or electromagnetic field probe to measure pipe thickness. Operators control it with a standard video game controller “Our initial target is just being able to get eyes in the pipe,” McArthur said. “The goal is to be able to inspect for corrosion or other types of damage like cracks or anything that would raise a concern.” With few access points in the Hanford pipe network and hundreds of feet of pipe with multiple 90-degree turns to navigate, this robot had to do what other devices couldn’t. “We wanted a flexible body to let the pipe sort of guide the robot,” Buerger said. “It’s really designed to conform to those pipe walls, roll in the pipe and steer and re-orient itself if needed. It must handle a lot of things like T-joints and even making decisions on which way to go.” Years of work The SPIINE robot has undergone several updates and revisions since the project began more than two years ago. Getting it just right has not been easy. “One of the first challenges was tires. We’re using elastomeric or stretchy materials for things like the wheels,” Buerger said. “We had to do a lot of experimentation with different compounds to figure out what would interface best with pipe walls.” They also had to consider the tiny motors, and the big mission. “We had to figure out what would do best at transmitting power efficiently,” Buerger said. “Remember you have really limited forces from those small motors, the robot must be able to move itself along and pull payloads.” The robot must also overcome obstacles protruding from the pipe walls and navigate loose matter such as liquid sludge, or caked deposits. Then there are the hundreds of feet it must travel in one trip. SPIINE is designed to use a single cable that can transmit power and data to and from the robot while also bearing mechanical loads. It’s also designed to allow multiple robots or propulsion modules to be tied together in a series and additional payloads to be attached. “There was a strong sort of experimental piece there that went with this,” Buerger said. “We had to tackle the idea of being able to propel the robot at multiple points along the cable. When you’re dealing with very long distances and a cable in between with multiple bends, there’s something called the capstan effect where basically, the more bends you go around, the more you build up force required to drag a cable. With multiple bends, it gets really bad, really fast.” Think about a hose getting wrapped around a tree or another object. You pull, but the harder you pull, the more it tightens, requiring greater force to free it. If you have multiple robots propelling the cable between the wraps, you reduce that effect. Challenges ahead The next step is to test the robot in the real world. Tests at Sandia have been successful but seeing SPIINE at work at Hanford site could reveal new challenges. The team already knows of some issues it will have to tackle, including developing a self-cleaning function that would enable the robot to wipe its camera lens or a clean dirty pipe wall. The team is also working on a built-in, fail-safe recovery system in case the robot becomes stuck or disabled. Researchers are also exploring the idea of designing microscale ultrasonic sensors that would fit on the robot because conventional sensors don’t fit through a 90-degree turn. For the team, this is an important project to perfect. “We are helping to keep the environment clean, so it’s the mission that is really satisfying,” Buerger said. “One of the most rewarding parts of being a robotics engineer is using technology to help keep people out of harm’s way. SPIINE is a great example of that,” McArthur said. “The US Department of Energy’s Office of Environmental Management face an enormous challenge in addressing the environmental legacy from decades of nuclear weapons development and government-sponsored nuclear energy research. If our work can help inform critical inspections, reduce uncertainty, and minimize risk to workers, then we are contributing to something much larger than the robot itself. That is the kind of impact that makes this work so fulfilling.”

articles.summary: London Stock Exchange-listed energy firm EnQuest has decided to exit the UK upstream arena to strengthen its focus on Southeast Asia.
articles.body: Business & Finance November 19, 2026 · 6 minutes ago $960 million deal enabling NEO NEXT+ to bring EnQuest’s UK North Sea business into its fold London Stock Exchange-listed energy firm EnQuest has decided to exit the UK upstream arena to strengthen its focus on Southeast Asia. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 4 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Magnus platform Source: EnQuest UK’s independent oil and gas producer NEO NEXT+ Energy is boosting its portfolio with the acquisition of EnQuest’s UK upstream business and associated infrastructure, as the seller accelerates its pivot toward Southeast Asia, following a series of acquisitions in Malaysia. EnQuest has entered into an agreement to sell its UK upstream business and associated infrastructure through the sale of EnQuest Britain to NEO NEXT+ Energy for total consideration of up to $960 million, encompassing $840 million in upfront cash consideration to be paid on completion, subject to customary closing adjustments, including working capital, together with up to $120 million contingent cash consideration. The proposed disposal is based on an economic effective date of January 1, 2027, and is subject to customary conditions, including, among others, regulatory approvals and completion of the firm’s acquisitions of participating interests in four PSCs in Malaysia, which remain on track to complete on December 31, 2026. These moves continue EnQuest’s strategic pivot to Southeast Asia as its primary operating region, creating a low-cost, highly resilient platform from which to pursue further near-term capital-efficient organic and inorganic growth. Following completion of the proposed disposal, EnQuest intends to repay debt drawn in connection with the proposed acquisitions, while retaining significant liquidity and financial flexibility to pursue material organic growth and further acquisition opportunities across the region. Related Articles Fossil Energy EnQuest makes $833 million play to expand its Southeast Asian oil & gas arsenal 3 min read " The resulting business will have a materially lower cost base and significantly enhanced balance sheet strength to pursue both organic investment and further value-accretive acquisitions across Southeast Asia, while supporting sustainable shareholder returns. We are immensely proud of what our teams have achieved in the UK and believe that NEO NEXT+’s combination of scale and track record as a leading North Sea operator, and diverse asset portfolio will enhance career opportunities for our people. We are committed to working closely with NEO NEXT+, our employees, joint venture partners and other stakeholders to ensure an orderly transition. " — Amjad Bseisu Chief Executive Officer of EnQuest The company’s board of directors believes the proposed disposal represents a significant step forward in the continued strategic evolution of EnQuest, crystallizing material value from the firm’s UK upstream portfolio, significantly strengthening its capital structure and completing the repositioning toward Southeast Asia. EnQuest took these steps to establish Southeast Asia as its primary operating region, where it sees significant opportunities for further high-return, capital-efficient growth, and maintain its established focus on operatorship and highly tangible reserves, deploying its operating capabilities and experienced asset teams to enhance value via a number of measures, including recovery factor improvement and conversion of 2C resources. In addition, the company believes this divestment and recent acquisitions provide a strengthened platform from which to accelerate further organic growth initiatives in Southeast Asia and capitalize on further inorganic growth opportunities across the region. The remaining EnQuest portfolio on a 2025 net participating interest basis, following completion of the proposed disposal and the acquisitions, is expected to benefit from around 70,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (boe/d) in the Southeast Asia business, with a unit opex of about $11/boe, a reduction of approximately 57% against its 2025 unit opex of $25/boe, generating a pro forma EBITDA of circa $500 million. While elaborating that production has grown further via the addition of low-cost Seligi 1b gas volumes in 2026, the firm emphasizes the substantial capital-efficient growth potential, including opportunities to leverage existing infrastructure, adding that its Southeast Asia capital investment is focused on high-return production enhancement activity, with minimal infrastructure investment required. The proposed disposal will involve the sale of all of the issued shares of EnQuest Britain, which through its subsidiaries holds the firm’s UK upstream assets, including Magnus , Kraken , and the Greater Kittiwake Area (operated), Golden Eagle (non-operated), and the undeveloped Bressay field and Bentley discovery. Additionally, the portfolio entails UK decommissioning and midstream assets, including EnQuest’s operating interest in the Sullom Voe Terminal , the Northern Leg Gas Pipeline , and the Ninian Pipeline system. Employees supporting these operations will transfer to the new owner as a result of the deal. EnQuest’s UK upstream assets contributed 31,122 boe/d of average net production (92% liquids and 8% gas) for the year ended December 31, 2025, when the portfolio comprised approximately 122 million boe of 2P reserves and 308 million boe of 2C resources. " The proposed disposal represents a significant repositioning of EnQuest, continuing the company’s transformation from a UK-focused operator into a business focused on high-quality assets in Southeast Asia, underpinned by a simple, strong capital structure. Following completion of both the proposed acquisitions and the proposed disposal, EnQuest will be a significant operator of scale, with its upstream portfolio focused solely on its 97% operated 2P asset base in Southeast Asia. " — EnQuest underlined. The completion of the divestment is expected in the first quarter of 2027, subject to conditions set out in the agreement, such as receipt of applicable regulatory approvals, including NSTA and NSIA approval and CMA clearance; completion of the company’s previously announced proposed acquisitions of participating interests offshore Malaysia; and other customary approvals and consents, including, amongst others, RBL lender consent and replacement of UK Decommissioning Security Agreements. Upon completion of the disposal, EnQuest will have interests in production, development, and exploration assets in Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei, and Indonesia, as well as Veri Energy, a wholly owned subsidiary, and associated CCUS interests, which sit outside this perimeter. FMD's Peterborough facility supplies Mission Bay Handling Systems for Canada’s River-class destroyer program, the United Kingdom’s Type 26 frigates and Australia’s Hunter-class frigates. Its capabilities include large-scale assembly, testing and integration of complex naval and undersea handling systems, as well as expertise in towed array winches, variable depth sonar systems and acoustic sensor handling equipment.

articles.body: Cool Carriers Welcomes Snow Land, First Reefer with Gate Rudder Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 19, 2026 © Cool Carriers Cool Carriers, the world’s largest operator of specialized reefer vessels, took delivery of Snow Land from Kitanihon Shipbuilding in Japan on November 12, 2026. The ice-class vessel is the world’s first specialized refrigerated cargo ship fitted with a gate rudder. The Gate Rudder System (GRS) is a marine propulsion and steering technology that replaces a traditional single rudder behind the propeller with two symmetrical, high-lift foil rudders positioned on either side of the propeller. At sea, water flowing over the blades generates additional forward thrust, so the main engine can maintain the same speed using less fuel and cutting CO₂ emissions on long ocean passages. In port, the crew can angle each blade separately for finer control when berthing. According to Wärtsilä, a licensee of the Gate Rudder technology, vessels equipped with it have reported fuel savings of up to 20%. For Snow Land, Kitanihon Shipbuilding reports that the ship’s overall design achieves a CO₂ intensity around 50% below the reference level for a vessel of her type and size. This figure is based on the Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI), calculated for operation on heavy fuel oil. Beyond the rudder, Snow Land is built for flexible, high-capacity cargo operations. She measures 162.5 meters in length and 25 meters in breadth, with a fully laden service speed of approximately 18 knots. Her holds provide 660,738 cubic feet (18,710 cubic metres) of refrigerated cargo space. Eight cooling zones allow fresh fruit and frozen goods to travel at different temperatures on the same voyage, within a range of −25°C to +15°C. On deck, she has slots for up to 168 forty-foot refrigerated containers. Snow Land is the third of seven vessels in Cool Carriers’ Snow-class program, following her sister ships Snow Flower and Snow Flake. The Snow-class newbuildings form part of Cool Carriers’ long-term fleet renewal strategy, strengthening its competitiveness in the specialized reefer market while improving operational efficiency and environmental performance, and setting a new direction for the industry. Four more Snow-class ships will join the fleet over the next two years.

articles.title: Red Sea returns are rewriting carrier reliability, not just transit times
articles.summary: The return of container services to the Red Sea is changing Asia–Europe schedules again. For shippers preparing 2027 contracts, the attraction is clear: Suez offers a shorter route than the Cape of Good Hope. articles.body: The return of container services to the Red Sea is changing Asia–Europe schedules again. For shippers preparing 2027 contracts, the attraction is clear: Suez offers a shorter route than the Cape of Good Hope. The harder question is whether the shorter passage will produce more dependable arrival windows. The transition is taking place service by service. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd moved their joint ME1 service, linking India and Europe, to the trans-Suez route from November, with the first westbound and eastbound sailings scheduled from Salalah on 4 November and Tangier on 13 November. On 17 November, Hapag-Lloyd announced that three further Gemini services, NE1, NE2 and NE3, would also return to Suez, with initial westbound transitions scheduled for December 2026 and January 2027. The sequence shows that the return is being managed through individual service decisions, not a single network-wide switch. For cargo owners, this distinction matters. A shorter sea passage changes the planned transit time. It does not, by itself, confirm that a vessel will arrive on schedule, that a transshipment connection will hold or that cargo will be available when expected. A Shorter Route Does Not Guarantee a Reliable Schedule Cape diversions extended Asia–Europe rotations and absorbed vessel capacity. Returning to Suez can release sailing days and help carriers redesign rotations. But the timetable also depends on port calls, vessel deployment, buffer time, terminal congestion, transshipment connections and the recovery of equipment flows. The Red Sea return is therefore unfolding against a wider reliability problem. Xeneta’s October 2026 Schedule Reliability Scorecard put global on-time arrivals at 24%, the lowest monthly average since July 2022. On the Far East–Europe trade, only 7% of vessels arrived on time, while average delay reached 9.0 days. The scorecard also found that Gemini services recorded 7% on-time arrivals on this lane, compared with 23% for non-alliance services. Gemini’s average delay was 9.4 days, against 6.8 days for Ocean Alliance and 7.8 days for MSC. These figures should not be read as evidence that the Suez return caused the delays. Xeneta points to broader pressures, including disruption at Asian ports, the effects of typhoons, vessel queues and changes in blank sailings. They do, however, show why shippers should avoid treating a shorter route as a proxy for better schedule performance. Reliability Is Specific to the Service and Direction A carrier’s network-wide reliability score can conceal substantial differences between individual services, port pairs and voyage directions. A service may use Suez on its westbound leg while retaining a Cape diversion eastbound. Another may return to the canal only after a particular sailing date. The service name alone is not enough to establish how a booked container will move. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd’s November changes illustrate this staged approach. The ME1 service has moved to Suez, while the NE1, NE2 and NE3 transitions are scheduled across different weeks from December into January. The carriers have said the planned dates remain subject to operational conditions. Their updates also make clear that further routing changes depend on the security situation. That qualification remains material. The Norwegian Maritime Authority’s October 30 notice kept ISPS Security Level 3 in force in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait for Norwegian vessels, with Level 2 applying in the southern Red Sea and northern Gulf of Aden. A carrier may therefore retain alternative routing options even after a service has returned to the shorter corridor. For a shipper, the relevant comparison is not simply which carrier has announced a Suez return. It is which specific service is scheduled to use the route, in which direction, from which voyage, and what contingency applies if the plan changes. What Shippers Should Test Before 2027 Contracts Reliability should be assessed through a consistent set of service-level measures rather than a carrier’s headline transit-time promise. Before committing cargo volumes, shippers and forwarders should examine: On-time performance by port pair and direction: Request a rolling 12-month record for the actual service and trade lane, not only a global carrier or alliance average. Delay severity: Compare average and median delay, and examine how often arrivals exceed the agreed delivery window. A high on-time percentage can still hide a small number of severe delays. Blank sailings and port omissions: Review cancellations, skipped calls, schedule revisions and changes to transshipment hubs. These can disrupt cargo plans even when the sailing that operates arrives on time. Routing and contingency terms: Confirm whether the carrier can switch between Suez and the Cape, how notice will be provided, and how additional transit time, surcharges or revised port rotations will be handled. End-to-end cargo availability: Track the time from vessel arrival to discharge, release and onward movement. A timely arrival does not guarantee that cargo will be ready for collection or connected to inland transport. The last point is important because the vessel schedule is only one part of the logistics chain. Vyansa Intelligence’s Global Captive Logistics Market Report estimates that transportation services account for around 40% of the global captive logistics market’s service-type segment. The report includes seaways and inland waterways within its transportation-mode coverage. This is not a measure of ocean-carrier reliability, but it illustrates the weight of transport execution within wider logistics networks, where vessel delays can affect inventory, warehouse slots and onward distribution. Shippers should also compare reliability data using the same provider and methodology across carriers. Schedule reliability datasets do not always use identical coverage or calculation rules, so combining scores from different providers can create misleading rankings. The most useful tender evidence is a like-for-like comparison of the service, direction, port pair and reporting period that the cargo will actually use. A 2027 Decision Based on Performance, Not the Map The return to Suez can shorten voyages and improve vessel utilisation, but those benefits will be realised unevenly as carriers adjust rotations and retain contingency options. Reliability will depend on how consistently each service operates through the transition, how quickly downstream port and equipment flows adapt, and whether security conditions allow the new routing to continue. For 2027 contracts, shippers should treat the announced route as one input, not the final verdict. The stronger choice will be the service that can demonstrate stable port rotations, controlled delays, transparent contingency arrangements and dependable cargo availability across the full journey. Shammi Thakur is the Research Director at Vyansa Intelligence, with over 15 years of experience in market research, strategic intelligence and industry analysis. His work includes maritime and logistics research, tracking industry developments, operational trends and the factors shaping shipping and supply chain decisions.

For shippers preparing 2027 contracts, the attraction is clear: Suez offers a shorter route than the Cape of Good Hope.
The harder question is whether the shorter passage will produce more dependable arrival windows.

articles.title: GONDAN Shipbuilders to Build Carbon-Fiber Electric Catamarans
articles.summary: GONDAN Shipbuilders has signed a contract with AB Göteborg-Styrsö Skärgardstrafik-Styrsöbolaget- to design and build three 100% electric passenger catamarans engineered to meet the operational and environmental standards of Northern European public transport.
articles.body: GONDAN Shipbuilders to Build Carbon-Fiber Electric Catamarans Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 19, 2026 © GONDAN Shipbuilders GONDAN Shipbuilders has signed a contract with AB Göteborg-Styrsö Skärgardstrafik-Styrsöbolaget- to design and build three 100% electric passenger catamarans engineered to meet the operational and environmental standards of Northern European public transport. Operating in Gothenburg's southern archipelago, the newbuilds form part of the 15-year operating contract awarded to Styrsöbolaget by Vasttrafik, the public transport authority of Västra Götalandsregionen responsible for public transit across the Gothenburg region and surrounding area. Built at GONDAN's dedicated composite facilities using carbon fiber, the three catamarans are optimized to minimize structural weight, achieve higher service speeds, lower energy consumption, and extend operational range in intensive daily commuter service-key requirements for high-efficiency, zero-emission ferry operations in Nordic waters. Adopting a holistic, multidisciplinary engineering approach, GONDAN's in-house technical office evaluated route profiles alongside shore-side grid capacity and power availability at each berthing point, integrating vessel displacement, service speed, and full-lifecycle durability to accurately size the battery systems and define the charging infrastructure requirements Designated with hull number C520 for the lead vessel and measuring 35 x 9 meters, each catamaran will accommodate 197 passengers (160 seated) and reach a service speed of 25 knots.

articles.summary: Boskalis Subsea Services has secured a long-term contract with Apache North Sea for what is described as one of the UK’s largest offshore...
articles.body: Decommissioning November 19, 2026 · 1 minute ago Boskalis Subsea Services joins one of 'UK’s largest offshore decommissioning programs' NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Boskalis Subsea Services via LinkedIn Boskalis Subsea Services has secured a long-term contract with Apache North Sea for what is described as one of the UK’s largest offshore decommissioning programs. Boskalis Subsea Services will deliver a comprehensive subsea decommissioning program covering subsea wells, subsea structures and associated pipelines and infrastructure, including the flushing, disconnection, recovery and disposal of all subsea infrastructure for the operator’s Forties and Beryl fields in the UK North Sea. “This contract marks another significant milestone as we continue to progress one of the UK’s largest offshore decommissioning programmes. As our Forties and Beryl assets move through the next stage of their lifecycle, we remain focused on delivering decommissioning safely, responsibly and efficiently, while drawing on the expertise of experienced partners to help achieve that," said Donald Martin , Vice President of Decommissioning at Apache. "Boskalis demonstrated the technical capability, collaborative approach and long-term commitment we were looking for throughout the tender process. By working together as one integrated team, we are building the foundations for a programme that will deliver value over the coming decade and support the responsible retirement of this significant North Sea infrastructure.” The company plans to establish a dedicated core team within Apache’s Aberdeen office, working closely with Apache personnel to support planning, engineering and project delivery. According to the firm, a predominantly ROV-led approach will be used across much of the campaign. “As the North Sea continues to evolve, decommissioning will play an increasingly important role in supporting the basin’s future. This programme draws on the full breadth of our subsea capability, combining engineering expertise, offshore execution, advanced ROV systems, remote operations and diving services to deliver safe and efficient outcomes for our clients," said Stuart Cameron , Managing Director of Boskalis Subsea Services. "We have invested significantly in developing these capabilities over recent years, and this award reflects the growing demand for integrated subsea solutions that can support large-scale decommissioning programmes from planning through to execution.” Related Articles News Boskalis Subsea Services wins its first decommissioning-specific contract with Shell 1 min read Reach the Offshore Energy industry in one go! articles.body: Cabling November 19, 2026 · 1 minute ago NKT’s Karlskrona offshore cable factory expansion set to start operations in Q2 2027 AB Adrijana Buljan Offshore Wind 1 minutes read LinkedIn X Email NKT (2025) NKT expects the additional production capacity at its high-voltage cable factory in Karlskrona, Sweden, to begin commercial operation and ramp up in the second quarter of 2027, slightly ahead of the original schedule, according to the company’s Q1-Q3 2026 interim report. The Danish cable manufacturer said installation and testing of machinery at the expanded facility had continued during the third quarter. The investment will increase Karlskrona’s production capacity for high-voltage subsea cables used in offshore wind farms and interconnector projects. The expansion includes a new factory and a third extrusion tower, which reached its full height of 200 metres in late 2024 . According to NKT, the tower is essential for manufacturing longer high-voltage cables, as it enables the insulation process required for their production. The Karlskrona expansion is part of NKT’s investment program in high-voltage production and installation capacity, announced in 2023. articles.title: Napier Port lifts earnings despite flat container volumes
articles.summary: Napier Port reported further earnings growth for the financial year ended 30 September 2026, supported by a stronger cargo mix, higher container revenue and its yield-management strategy. Revenue increased by 11.7% to NZ$176.2 million, compared with NZ$157.7 million in the previous financial year. Reported net profit...
articles.body: Napier Port reported further earnings growth for the financial year ended 30 September 2026, supported by a stronger cargo mix, higher container revenue and its yield-management strategy. Revenue increased by 11.7% to NZ$176.2 million, compared with NZ$157.7 million in the previous financial year. Reported net profit after tax rose by 15% to NZ$35.5 million. Underlying net profit increased by 30.5% to NZ$36.9 million. The port’s result from operating activities reached NZ$75.7 million, representing an increase of 17.9%. Its operating margin improved from 40.7% to 43%. “2026 was a strong year of service delivery and continued earnings growth for Napier Port,” said Blair O’Keeffe, Chair of Napier Port. “The result reflects the strength of our diverse cargo base, continued progress with our yield and cost management strategies, and the resilience of Hawke’s Bay’s primary sector,” he added. Container throughput remains at 250,000 TEU Container volumes remained unchanged at approximately 250,000 TEU. Full container volumes increased by 5%, supported by higher exports of apples, meat and timber and increased imports of paper products and fertiliser. Empty and other container movements declined by 5.6%, primarily because of lower transshipment activity. Average container services revenue per TEU increased by 18.9%. Napier Port attributed the rise to a higher-yielding cargo mix, tariff and levy adjustments, increased vessel-call revenue and growth at its Viewpoint supply-chain business. Viewpoint recorded higher volumes during the year as more customers outside the region moved cargo through Napier Port. Much of this cargo travelled by rail between Napier and Palmerston North. Bulk cargo volumes decreased by 2.7% to 3.32 million tonnes. Log exports fell by 2.8% to 2.6 million tonnes, while bulk imports declined by 7.2%. Cruise calls decreased from 78 to 55 and generated NZ$6.5 million in revenue, down 20.8% from the previous year. Autonomous terminal operations planned for 2027 Napier Port continued its three-year investment programme during the financial year. Its ShoreTension mooring system entered operation at 6 Wharf, while the new dredger KAPUKA was launched. The port’s container terminal transformation project also moved into operational testing. Napier Port has activated its private 5G network and is testing its first battery-electric truck. It plans to introduce autonomous truck-and-trailer operations at the container terminal during 2027. The company is also assessing future container crane replacements, with a final investment decision expected during the 2027 financial year. Napier Port expects an underlying result from operating activities of between NZ$80 million and NZ$85 million in FY2027, assuming current market conditions continue.

REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration/File Photo By Yongchang Chin Nov 19, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Some of the world’s top commodity-trading houses are in talks to secure more long-term supplies of Qatari crude, seeking to build on their success at shuttling oil out of the Persian Gulf during the Iran-US war. The companies spoke with state-owned QatarEnergy this month to ask for volumes to be supplied over 2027, according to people involved in the discussions. Grades of interest centered on Qatar Marine and Land varieties, they said, asking not to be named as the talks are private. Crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have picked up in recent months, despite the stalemate between Washington and Tehran and continued attacks on vessels. The flows have helped to drag prices lower, with traders proving adept at moving volumes and shouldering the risks, while some refiners have been more wary. That’s opening up opportunities for 2027. Qatar — which also provided almost a fifth of the world’s liquefied natural gas before the war damaged infrastructure and hampered shipments — is a located within the Persian Gulf, and its shipments must transit Hormuz. Term deals allow for contracted volumes to be supplied over longer periods, handing the supplier and buyer more certainty than relying on spot shipments. With a little more than a month left before 2027 contracts start in January, several Asian refiners and traders are still in talks with producers like QatarEnergy and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. Adnoc has also been willing to sell more term supplies to trading companies next year, Bloomberg has reported. QatarEnergy typically inks yearlong supply deals with refiners, but such discussions for next year’s term volumes have been slowed down by issues surrounding shipping crude through Hormuz, the people said. The company didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Some traders already buy Qatari crude on a term basis, but the volumes have mainly centered on the flagship Al-Shaheen grade. Others typically secure cargoes via monthly tenders, a regular fixture before the Iran war, and one which QatarEnergy has pushed to reinstate. During the conflict, commodity houses — including Vitol Group, Mercuria Energy Group and Trafigura Group, as well as the arms of producers such as TotalEnergies SE and Adnoc — have assumed greater prominence in ensuring the continuity of energy flows between the Persian Gulf and Asia. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P.
