articles.title: Lynch Yacht Crew Unaware of Wind Risk Before Fatal Sinking, UK Report Finds
articles.summary: The crew of British tech tycoon Mike Lynch's yacht, which sank off Sicily in 2024 killing him and six others, was unaware of its vulnerability to strong winds because the risk had never been assessed, a British investigation found on Thursday.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network A drone view shows floating crane ships HEBO LIFT 10 and HEBO LIFT 2 recovering the "Bayesian" yacht of British tech entrepreneur Mike Lynch, who died when the yacht sank off Porticello, near Palermo, Sicily, Italy, June 20, 2025. REUTERS/Danilo Arnone TPX IMAGES OF THE DAY By Paul Sandle LONDON, Nov 19 (Reuters) – The crew of British tech tycoon Mike Lynch’s yacht, which sank off Sicily in 2024 killing him and six others, was unaware of its vulnerability to strong winds because the risk had never been assessed, a British investigation found on Thursday. The 56-meter-long (184-foot) Bayesian was moored off Porticello, near Palermo, in August 2024 when it was hit by a violent downburst in a storm, forcing it onto its side, where it began taking on water. Unable to right itself, the yacht flooded, capsized and sank around 18 minutes later, Britain’s Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) said. Lynch, a British tech entrepreneur , had been celebrating his acquittal on 15 counts of fraud two months earlier over the sale of his company Autonomy to Hewlett Packard. He was sailing with his family and friends who supported him during the US trial. His 18-year-old daughter Hannah died, along with lawyer Chris Morvillo and his wife Neda, banker Jonathan Bloomer and his wife Judy, and chef Recaldo Thomas. The yacht was vulnerable to violent winds and was probably knocked over by gusts of more than 117 kilometers (73 miles) per hour, British investigators said in 2025. Thursday’s report by the MAIB, which was not designed to determine liability, said the yacht’s vulnerability to wind when operating under engine power had never been assessed, leaving its 10-person crew unaware of a critical risk. Its 72-meter mast and furled sails contributed significantly to the risk, the report said. The yacht’s stability information book did not identify its vulnerabilities when anchored with its sails furled and keel raised, meaning neither the owner nor crew knew of the danger. “The vulnerability of Bayesian to wind heeling moments while in the motoring condition had never been assessed, resulting in the crew being unaware of a critical risk to the vessel and unable to take account of it in their operations,” it said. The report said the safety of the six guests and nine crew members who escaped the yacht and were rescued relied heavily on the training, experience and initiative of individual crew members. The Bayesian was built in 2008 by Perini Navi, an Italian luxury yacht maker owned by the Italian Sea Group. The company in 2024 said the sinking was due to a chain of human errors, and if the crew had shut all doors and hatches, turned on the engine, lifted the anchor, lowered the keel and turned the yacht to face the wind, it would have suffered no damage. articles.body: India Eases Vessel Age Restrictions to Strengthen Domestic Shipping Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 19, 2026 © Asanee / Adobe Stock India has relaxed rules allowing vessels more than 20 years old to be registered under its flag, according to a government order, potentially expanding its domestic shipping fleet and reducing reliance on foreign carriers. The new rules lay out conditions for 15- to 20-year-old oil tankers to join the Indian registry or avail themselves of the Indian flag, said the order by the federal maritime agency, the Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA). For vessels above 20 years of age, including oil tankers, general cargo vessels and offshore fleet entry into the Indian flag registry requires approval by a five-member committee of DGMA to ensure the quality of ships. There are no exit age limits for Indian-flag ships, said the order issued on Wednesday. Previously, vessels older than 20 years were not permitted to register under the Indian flag. India, a key consumer of oil, gas and other products, largely relies on foreign carriers for imports. The move will improve India's access to ships in times of crisis. Indian-flagged vessels get priority in securing certain government and state-run companies' cargo contracts before foreign-flagged ships are considered. (Reuters - Reporting by Nidhi Verma)

articles.body: International consultancy Steer has completed the acquisition of Mercator International, expanding its advisory capabilities in the ports, maritime and freight sectors. Based in Kirkland, Washington, Mercator advises port authorities, terminal operators, shipping lines, logistics companies and investors on commercial strategy and infrastructure transactions. The acquisition strengthens Steer’s presence in North America while expanding its expertise in maritime infrastructure and investment advisory. Mercator will become part of Steer’s North America division, led by Herb Higginbotham. However, the company will continue operating under its existing name, maintaining its current projects and customer relationships. Acquisition expands maritime advisory capabilities Founded in 2000, Mercator has completed more than 150 commercial due diligence projects. It has also advised over 40 investors and financial institutions on transactions worldwide. Its previous assignments include advising the Ports of Seattle and Tacoma on the formation of the Northwest Seaport Alliance. The company has also supported the Quebec Port Authority on a new container terminal project and advised the Macquarie-led consortium on its acquisition of Long Beach Container Terminal. Through the acquisition, Steer will combine Mercator’s maritime expertise with its wider capabilities in rail, freight, infrastructure planning and investment advisory. “Mercator brings an excellent team of ports and maritime experts that will strengthen our offer well beyond North America,” said Hugh Jones, CEO, Steer. “As our second acquisition this year, it’s a clear signal of where Steer is heading as we deliver on our ambitious growth plans,” Jones added. The transaction marks Steer’s fourth acquisition since 2021. Its previous acquisitions include Fourth Economy in the United States, alongside Amberside Advisors and Evolution Infrastructure in the United Kingdom. Mercator will also work closely with Steer’s existing ports and maritime practice, led by Alberto Preti in Italy and Steve Wray in the United Kingdom. Steve Rothberg, founder of Mercator International, said the combination would allow the company to offer clients a broader range of services while maintaining its established approach to maritime advisory. articles.title: Torm hits back at Hafnia over rejected merger bids
articles.summary: Danish product tanker giant Torm has hit back at Hafnia following its abandoned takeover pursuit, revealing that it rejected several merger proposals from its rival because they offered no meaningful premium and substantially undervalued the company. The Jacob Meldgaard-led owner broke its silence after BW...
articles.body: Europe Tankers Torm hits back at Hafnia over rejected merger bids Adis Ajdin November 19, 2026 0 6 2 minutes read Torm Torm Danish product tanker giant Torm has hit back at Hafnia following its abandoned takeover pursuit, revealing that it rejected several merger proposals from its rival because they offered no meaningful premium and substantially undervalued the company. The Jacob Meldgaard-led owner broke its silence after BW Group-backed Hafnia announced plans to exit its near-20% stake, bringing an end to its attempts to combine two of the world’s largest product tanker operators. Torm confirmed that Hafnia had submitted a number of conditional, all-share proposals, but said none offered an effective premium for control. Its board, following discussions with financial and legal advisers, unanimously rejected each proposal and informed Hafnia of its decision on every occasion. Torm chairman Simon Mackenzie Smith defended the decision, arguing that Hafnia had failed to recognise the company’s operating performance and future prospects. “The proposals from Hafnia fundamentally failed to recognize that track record and the significant future value embedded in the One Torm platform,” he said. The response comes after Hafnia chief executive Søren Steenberg Jensen announced that the company was walking away from its consolidation ambitions, having failed to secure Torm’s support. Jensen said the company’s approaches had not been reciprocated and that continued resistance would undermine the potential benefits of bringing the two tanker groups together. Torm’s response makes clear that the disagreement was not over whether proposals had been received, but over their valuation and the absence of a meaningful takeover premium. The Danish owner did not disclose the proposed exchange ratios or other financial terms of Hafnia’s approaches. Hafnia, which spent more than $500m building its position in Torm, now intends to dispose of its entire holding of approximately 20.36m shares, representing around 19.8% of the company. The stake was valued at $686.6m based on Torm’s November 17 closing share price. Hafnia’s preferred route is to distribute the shares directly to its own shareholders through a special dividend, giving them the option of retaining or selling their individual holdings. The proposal remains subject to third-party cooperation, with Hafnia setting November 25 as the deadline for determining whether the distribution can proceed. If the necessary arrangements cannot be completed, Hafnia plans to pay a regular cash dividend under its existing policy and consider alternative ways to exit its Torm investment. articles.title: Europe and Central Asia are closing the distance. Growing trade needs efficient logistics
articles.summary: The economies of Central Asia grew by a combined total of more than 6% in 2025, according to estimates by the World Bank and the Eurasian Development Bank. This growth is increasingly visible both in trade volumes and in expanding transport options. This November marks three years since SUUS established its presence...
articles.body: The economies of Central Asia grew by a combined total of more than 6% in 2025, according to estimates by the World Bank and the Eurasian Development Bank. This growth is increasingly visible both in trade volumes and in expanding transport options. This November marks three years since SUUS established its presence in Almaty, and for the past six months we have also been operating in Tashkent. This time has given us an even better understanding of the region and confirmed our view that it is an attractive direction for growth, both for Polish companies and for other global players. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are the two largest economies in Central Asia and the pillars of its development. Uzbekistan closed 2025 with GDP growth of 7.7%, according to the National Statistics Committee, and Kazakhstan with 6.5%, according to preliminary data from the Bureau of National Statistics. In both countries, logistics grew faster than the economy as a whole. In Uzbekistan, the value of transport services rose by 10.8%, while in Kazakhstan the transport and warehousing sector expanded by 20.4%, more than three times faster than GDP. From our perspective, these are the figures that matter most. They show that rising demand is already translating into real flows of goods and the development of the transport and logistics sector. Trade with the European Union is growing in both directions In 2024, Poland exported goods worth EUR 1.6 billion to Central Asia, EUR 0.6 billion more than in 2021. Two-thirds of these exports go to Kazakhstan, according to a report by the Polish Economic Institute (PIE). Polish and European companies from the household appliances, construction, fashion and pharmaceutical sectors increasingly treat Central Asia as a target market. These are precisely the industries we work with on this route, handling their shipments to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. Trade is also supported by institutions and carriers. The Polish Investment and Trade Agency (PAIH) has an office in Astana and is accelerating the opening of a representative office in Tashkent, while since May LOT Polish Airlines has been flying to Almaty, its third destination in the region after Astana and Tashkent. The flow in the opposite direction is just as clear. According to the European Commission, the EU accounts for nearly a third of Central Asia’s exports and is its main export market. The region delivers to the EU mainly oil, gas, metals, and cotton fibre. Since 2021, Uzbekistan has benefited from the EU’s GSP+ trade preferences, and in October 2025 it signed an Enhanced Partnership and Cooperation Agreement with the EU. For Central Asian exporters, Central and Eastern Europe, including Poland, is a natural gateway to the EU market. The region is accelerating investment in roads and rail Kazakhstan is preparing the largest infrastructure programme in its history. By 2029, the country plans to invest more than USD 14 billion in projects covering roads, railways, airports and energy, among others. The effects of earlier investments are already visible. According to Kazakhstan’s Minister of Transport, 94% of national roads meet the required quality standards, which translates into shorter and more predictable journey times. At the same time, countries in the region are expanding their networks for international freight. The Bakhty–Ayagoz line, with a third rail border crossing to China, is due to be completed by 2027. Closest to completion is the Darbaza–Maktaaral line in southern Kazakhstan, near the border with Uzbekistan, where traffic is set to start by the end of this year. The line will relieve the key route via Saryagash station to Tashkent. This matters for growing trade, as rail freight between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan rose by 16% in 2025. The new airport in Tashkent is being developed by Uzbekistan together with investors from Saudi Arabia, Japan and South Korea, a sign that companies from the world’s leading economies are committing to these markets for the long term. The Middle Corridor, the route from China through Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus to Central and Eastern Europe, is becoming increasingly important for transport between Asia and Europe. According to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport, volumes on this route grew from 0.8 to 4.5 million tonnes per year over seven years. Infrastructure is being developed as well: a new container hub has opened in the port of Aktau, and the expansion of the Dostyk–Moyynty rail line is set to increase its capacity fivefold. Meanwhile, a new berth is under construction at the Georgian port of Poti, which will ultimately raise its capacity to 3 million tonnes. In its October report on the Middle Corridor, the World Bank points out that the route’s potential will depend not only on infrastructure investment, but also on shorter waiting times at borders and simpler documentation. Cargo changes transport mode several times along the way and passes through numerous transshipments, while strong winds at the port of Aktau and winter snowfall continue to reduce operational efficiency. For companies using this route, transit time and efficient customs clearance remain critical. The advantage therefore goes to an operator that knows local conditions, plans the entire supply chain and takes responsibility for every transshipment. Successful expansion starts with a local partner Foreign investors in Central Asia need local know-how above all else. European companies entering Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are looking for a partner who understands local realities: business culture, market regulations, customs procedures, and settlements in local currency. Businesses from Central Asia targeting customers in Europe, in turn, need a logistics operator present in EU countries. At SUUS, we bring these two perspectives together. At our branches in Almaty and Tashkent, we provide road, rail, air and sea freight, intermodal solutions, warehousing, and customs services. Having our own structures in Central Asia means that solutions are designed by local teams who know the market and its conditions. The advantage in the region will go to operators that are present on both sides of the corridor and operate efficiently in all of its markets. Today, we are transferring three years of experience from Kazakhstan to Uzbekistan. For us, both markets are part of a single CEECA bridge linking China, Central Asia and Central and Eastern Europe. We look to the coming years with great optimism: if investments in rail and airports are delivered on schedule and border procedures are simplified, trade between Europe and Central Asia will have room to grow even faster. Andrzej Kozłowski, Member of the Management Board, Rohlig SUUS Logistics

articles.title: Sanctioned Tankers Carry 60% of Russian Oil in October: Monthly Intelligence Report
articles.summary: This analysis was produced by Windward’s Maritime Intelligence Operations Center (MIOC), a mission-critical capability powered by Windward’s maritime intelligence experts and operating as a seamless extension of your team. This is a sample of what we deliver. Vessel identifiers and ownership entities have been...
articles.body: Sanctioned Tankers Carry 60% of Russian Oil in October: Monthly Intelligence Report in International Shipping News 19/11/2026 This analysis was produced by Windward’s Maritime Intelligence Operations Center (MIOC), a mission-critical capability powered by Windward’s maritime intelligence experts and operating as a seamless extension of your team. This is a sample of what we deliver. Vessel identifiers and ownership entities have been redacted for external distribution; AIS-based assessments are probabilistic and intended solely as decision support, and nothing herein should be construed as evidence of wrongdoing by any vessel, company, or individual. For intelligence tailored to your operational theater, visit the MIOC page. Sanctioned Tankers Carry 60% of Russian Oil in October Sixty percent of Russian oil was shipped on sanctioned tankers throughout October, supported by a rising number of new shadow fleet entrants over 2026 that are being used to offset freight logistics inefficiencies and restrictions. Analysis of tankers calling at Russian ports to load crude, fuel oil and refined products last month found that EU-owned tankers shipped 14% of volumes, one of the lowest percentages recorded this year. Unsanctioned shadow fleet tankers accounted for 21% of all oil shipments, according to Windward analysis using data from Vortexa. Sanctioned tankers were mostly used for crude shipments (69% of barrels shipped), followed by refined products (42%) and fuel oil (30%). The overall figure of 60% carried on sanctioned tankers compares with 55% in September and 67% in March. Russia Secures New Unsanctioned Tonnage The October numbers underscore the rapidly changing composition of the sanctions-circumventing shadow fleet, and Russia’s ability to secure new, unsanctioned tonnage to support its freight logistics. Tankers that are sanctioned are reflagging to Russia and changing registered ownership to SVPs in China, Hong Kong, and Russia. Meanwhile, new companies are being formed to buy and deploy fresh and existing shadow fleet tonnage that has yet to be targeted by regulators. Naval Boardings Push Sanctioned Tankers To Reflag to Russian Of the 143 sanctioned tankers tracked calling at Russian Baltic, Black Sea, Arctic and Far East ports in October, 48% (69 ships) were flagged with Russia. Of those 69 ships, 31 have switched to the Russian flag in the past six months. The reflagging was triggered by a new strategy implemented by EU and UK naval forces over 2026 to board and interdict stateless or falsely flagged tankers. The remainder of sanctioned tonnage is flagged with Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Sierra Leone, or Oman. These ship registries continue to provide services to UK- or EU-sanctioned tankers, but not U.S.-sanctioned. No falsely flagged tonnage was noted loading Russian oil this month, the fourth consecutive month. There are several Russia-linked falsely flagged tankers observed loitering in the Mediterranean but do not appear to be active in shipping oil. Unsanctioned Tankers Step In to Supplement the Shadow Fleet The EU and UK have together blacklisted nearly 700 shadow fleet tankers over the past two-and-a-half years, disrupting the supply chain. Sanctions make it harder — but not impossible — for these ships to continue trading without links to Western marine service providers. The rise in unsanctioned shadow fleet tankers to replace and/or supplement the work of the inefficient sanctioned fleet is of particular interest, especially since EU regulations are in place that are designed to prevent sales of second-hand vessels for Russia trading. How Windward Defines the Unsanctioned Shadow Fleet Unsanctioned shadow fleet tankers are defined as those aged 15 years or over, solely deployed in Russian trades (including those undertaking two consecutive Russian oil loadings since a change in ownership was noted), with registered ownership and management hidden behind companies in jurisdictions where the beneficial owner cannot be traced. There were 41 unsanctioned shadow fleet tankers tracked shipping Russian oil in October. Of these, nine did not have P&I insurance with marine insurers that were part of the International Group. Of the remaining that did have International Group insurance, 88% were insured with two P&I clubs. There is no suggestion of wrongdoing by marine insurers. The G7 Oil Price Cap allows marine service providers to ship Russian oil to third countries if the price at which oil is sold is below a cap. New Shadow Fleet Clusters Emerge in 2026 The shadow fleet has evolved over the past four years, with tankers having multiple changes of registered owners, flags, and ISM managers across countries and jurisdictions to obfuscate beneficial ownership and evade sanctions. New clusters observed this year include what Windward has called the “Kowloon Cluster,” a group of 45-plus tankers linked by a Hong Kong-based nominee director and Azerbaijan ISM managers. All but three tankers are sanctioned. A UAE-Based Manager Amasses 20 Unsanctioned Tankers The newest cluster observed is a UAE-based cluster of 20 tankers, all unsanctioned. The fleet of 20 Russia-trading tankers began amassing in February via the ISM management of a newly formed United Arab Emirates-based entity. The company gives its address at serviced offices that overlook a racecourse in Dubai. The twenty ships moved to the company’s management between February and October this year. Six of them were unsanctioned but long-established shadow fleet players and connected to two sanctioned clusters. These shipping companies were disbanded in 2023 and linked to Rosneft and Lukoil. Eleven ships were sold directly to the company by EU-owned companies this year. Some but not all had already been deployed in shipping Russian oil under the G7 Oil Price Cap and continued to do so. Ajman-Based Shipmanager Takes Over Five Russia-Trading Tankers An Ajman-based shipmanager manages five shadow fleet tankers, all with registered ownership in China. All five tankers are unsanctioned and have been deployed in Russia trading for well over 18 months. They all entered management between February and May. Russia Imports Fuel as Refinery Attacks Cut Capacity Russian diesel and jet fuel exports over October were tracked by Vortexa at about 350,000 bpd, more than double September’s volumes, at 160,000 bpd. Before Ukraine attacks on Russian refineries accelerated in mid-2026, middle distillate export volumes were at about 800,000 bpd. Russia reportedly extended export bans on gasoline to diesel in July to address domestic shortfalls after attacks on refineries over 2026 left 51% of capacity offline, according to Ukraine’s Defense Ministry as of October 4. Domestic shortages saw Russia importing diesel and gasoline from July, with 115,000 bpd tracked arriving in August, just under 100,000 bpd in September and 70,000 bpd in October. Gasoil exported from a storage terminal at Morocco shipped most of the ~750,000 barrels of gasoil and diesel that were discharged at Russian Baltic ports last month. The U.S. Diesel Waiver Has Yet to Deliver a Cargo In response to a looming global diesel shortage, the U.S. government announced a US import sanctions waiver on Russian diesel on October 9. Despite the waiver, no Russian diesel cargoes have been tracked arriving in the U.S. amid political, compliance and enforcement challenges, especially if tankers are sanctioned by the UK or EU. One likely candidate, a Malta-flagged tanker, reversed course on November 10 about 450 nautical miles from Philadelphia, the probable destination, and had yet to signal a new destination seven days later. Diesel prices remain well above the $100/bbl G7 Oil Price Cap, with global assessments from price reporting agencies in the 190-200/bbl range over the month of October. There were 11 diesel cargoes loaded on tankers with EU ownership identified by Windward using Vortexa data extracted in early November. In order to remain price cap-compliant, Russian oil traders would have sold the cargo at half the price they could have secured in the global market. High Urals Price Tests Price Cap Enforcement According to the Russian Ministry of Economic Development, the average sales price of Urals crude over October was $101.46/barrel. This is 130% above the EU price cap of $44.10 per barrel. The ministry reached its assessment by averaging the price reported by the global price reporting agency, Argus. Argus assessments are used by oil traders worldwide. Like diesel, the high Urals price provides compliance and enforcement challenges for marine service providers with EU, UK, or U.S. exposure. Compliance rests on attestation documents that are provided by the buyer and seller of the oil and cannot be verified by all parties in the marine service chain. Some 7% (8.2 million barrels) of Urals shipped in October were on 12 EU-owned tankers, according to analysis. Source: Windward 2026-11-19 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.summary: US corn-based ethanol could offer shipowners a cheaper route to reducing greenhouse gas emissions than low-carbon methanol and ammonia, potentially opening a new marine fuel market for American producers as the global fleet of methanol-capable vessels expands, according to a study released last week. Ethanol could...
articles.body: US ethanol offers lower GHG abatement costs than methanol, ammonia: study in International Shipping News 19/11/2026 US corn-based ethanol could offer shipowners a cheaper route to reducing greenhouse gas emissions than low-carbon methanol and ammonia, potentially opening a new marine fuel market for American producers as the global fleet of methanol-capable vessels expands, according to a study released last week. Ethanol could abate about 2.09 metric tons of CO2 equivalent for every $1,000 spent on fuel, compared with 1.30 mt for low-carbon methanol and 1.73 mt for low-carbon ammonia, the Maritime Ethanol & Methanol Alliance, an initiative by the nonprofit Global Centre for Green Fuels, said in the study. MEMA estimated ethanol’s well-to-wake greenhouse gas intensity at 34.9 grams of CO2e/megajoule, compared with 15 gCO2e/MJ for low-carbon methanol and 10 gCO2e/MJ for low-carbon ammonia. Emissions abatement was calculated against a heavy fuel oil baseline of 93.3 gCO2e/MJ. “Ethanol is a commercially viable fuel when compared to other fuels … [it] delivers maximum carbon abatement per dollar of fuel expenditure among commercially available, scalable marine fuels,” according to the study. In the study, based on classification society ABS’s technical analysis, MEMA assumed US corn ethanol prices on a free-on-board Houston basis at $750/mt, equivalent to $1,125/mt of very low sulfur fuel oil on an energy-adjusted basis. That compared with $1,200/mt, or $2,424/mt on a VLSFO-equivalent basis, for low-carbon methanol and $900/mt, or $1,945/mt VLSFOe, for low-carbon ammonia. VLSFO was assumed at $590/mt. The study’s indicative mid-2026 prices showed ethanol remained substantially more expensive than conventional bunkers but offered lower costs than other low-carbon alternatives. Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed FOB Houston ethanol barge prices at 202.25 cents/gallon on Nov. 11, roughly equivalent to $677/mt. Delivered low-carbon methanol bunker prices in the Houston Ship Channel were $1,146.57/mt on the same day, according to Platts. US ethanol supply The US produced 16.4 billion gallons of ethanol in 2025, against an installed capacity of 18.5 billion gallons/year, leaving about 2 billion gallons of spare capacity, according to the study. US ethanol production capacity could expand to 18 billion-20 billion gallons/year by 2030 and 23 billion-26 billion gallons/year by 2035, supported by efficiency improvements, cellulosic production and new facilities, MEMA said. The study estimated that capturing 1% of international shipping’s fuel consumption with ethanol would require approximately 1 billion gallons annually, while a 5% share would require around 5 billion gallons annually. Ethanol, which has chemical and combustion properties similar to those of methanol, could generally be used in engines designed to run on methanol. The methanol-fueled fleet is expanding, with 157 vessels in service and more than 160 on order as of October 2026, according to S&P Global Maritime Portal data cited in the report. “Ethanol is moving beyond pilots, and this study shows the United States has the production base and export infrastructure to supply shipping at scale,” Global Centre for Green Fuels Managing Director Clarence Woo said in a statement. A.P. Moller-Maersk, one of the largest container lines, has been testing ethanol and ethanol-methanol blends in its methanol-capable fleet, progressing from a 10% ethanol blend to E100. On Sept. 28, the company’s 9,000 twenty-foot-equivalent-unit container ship, Tangier Maersk, completed the first commercial ship-to-ship bunkering of US corn ethanol in Houston. Kirby Corp. transported and bunkered the fuel. Regulatory uncertainty Regulatory uncertainty remains over the treatment of crop-based ethanol, although the International Maritime Organization has made progress toward recognizing specific production pathways. In May, the IMO agreed to include Brazilian second-crop corn ethanol in its draft revised lifecycle GHG assessment guidelines. The UN agency is still considering how indirect land-use change should be accounted for in other types of ethanol. Paula Nava, director of sustainability at Marquis Energy, a US ethanol producer, told Platts that IMO regulators should take fuel availability and existing national standards into consideration when defining sustainability criteria. “We should have a more flexible approach to what sustainability criteria is about,” Nava said. Under FuelEU Maritime, conventional crop-based ethanol continues to face less favorable regulatory treatment than advanced biofuels. “The next challenge is consistency,” Woo said, calling for standardized marine fuel specifications, traceable feedstocks and robust chain-of-custody systems. MEMA’s members include Bunker Holding, Raizen, Longi and Idemitsu, among other fuel producers, shipowners, ports, engine makers and classification societies. articles.title: Fincantieri’s WASS signs underwater defence agreement in India
articles.summary: Fincantieri’s subsidiary WASS Submarine Systems has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with India’s Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL) to explore cooperation in underwater defence systems. articles.body: Fincantieri’s subsidiary WASS Submarine Systems has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with India’s Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL) to explore cooperation in underwater defence systems. The agreement was signed during the Defence Industrial Cooperation Dialogue in New Delhi. It establishes a framework for potential industrial collaboration involving heavyweight torpedoes and torpedo countermeasure systems. The two companies will examine opportunities to develop manufacturing and technical support capabilities in India. Agreement targets local production and technical support The proposed cooperation covers several stages of underwater defence system production. These include component manufacturing, energetic sections, subassemblies, final assembly and factory testing. The companies will also explore maintenance and in-service support activities, allowing potential cooperation to extend beyond initial production. Under the agreement, WASS will contribute its experience in underwater defence technology, while BDL will provide its established industrial capabilities in India. The partnership aims to strengthen local manufacturing expertise and support India’s long-term development of domestic underwater defence capabilities. For Fincantieri, the agreement represents another step in expanding its industrial relationships in the Indian market. WASS previously secured a contract to supply torpedoes to the Indian Navy, strengthening its position in the country’s naval defence sector. The latest agreement builds on that presence by examining opportunities for broader industrial cooperation. However, the MoU does not constitute a confirmed manufacturing contract. The companies have not disclosed an investment value, production volumes or an implementation timetable.

The newbuild is scheduled to begin operations offshore Brazil in late 2028. Paratus has meanwhile narrowed its focus to the Brazilian subsea market following the completion of the sale of its Mexican jackup drilling business in July. Both companies stressed that the strategic review may not result in a transaction and that neither partner has decided to sell the business. However, Paratus has appointed Pareto Securities as its financial adviser, while Vantris has engaged J.P. Morgan to make a more informed decision. articles.title: AlloySelect relaunches at Offshore Energy 2026 with new CCS screening preview
articles.summary: Originally developed by OGC Energy in 2018, AlloySelect is now being relaunched with enhanced corrosion assessment and materials selection capabilities, alongside a new CCS module designed specifically for CO2 transport and storage applications.
articles.body: Branded Content November 19, 2026 · 30 minutes ago AlloySelect relaunches at Offshore Energy 2026 with new CCS screening preview Originally developed by OGC Energy in 2018, AlloySelect is now being relaunched with enhanced corrosion assessment and materials selection capabilities, alongside a new CCS module designed specifically for CO2 transport and storage applications. Written in partnership with OGC Energy 4 minutes read LinkedIn X Email OGC Energy The decisions behind the material Before engineers choose a material, they need confidence in the conditions against which it is being selected. Temperature, pressure, CO2, H2S, water chemistry and expected operating life all influence the assessment. A change in one assumption can alter the corrosion estimate, the materials shortlist or the level of further engineering required. That challenge is familiar to oil and gas projects. It is also increasingly relevant to carbon capture and storage (CCS), where engineers must consider the composition of transported CO2 streams, impurity specifications and the implications for equipment, pipelines and storage infrastructure. The calculations matter, but so does the ability to explain what was assumed and why a screening decision was reached. Eight years of practical engineering experience OGC Energy first developed AlloySelect in 2018 to bring its corrosion and materials engineering experience into a practical digital tool. Since then, the platform has been used to support clients working through corrosion assessment and materials selection questions. Feedback from that use has informed its relaunch for a new phase of energy projects. The objective remains straightforward: make early-stage corrosion and materials decisions easier to explore, repeat and communicate without taking engineering judgement out of the process. The refreshed offering brings together Evaluate and Select, with a new CCS screening preview introduced at Offshore Energy Exhibition & Conference (OEEC) 2026 in Amsterdam. Evaluate: make the assumptions visible AlloySelect Evaluate helps engineers estimate CO2 corrosion rates and see how the selected operating conditions affect the result. The interface brings inputs and outputs together, including calculated pH, corrosion rate, inhibited corrosion rate, corrosion allowance and environmental severity classification. Saved results and batch processing support repeated assessments across different cases. This makes a practical impact at the beginning of a project. Instead of presenting a corrosion-rate number in isolation, an engineer can examine the assumptions behind it and use the result as a starting point for the wider materials and corrosion-control discussion. Select: screen materials against actual service conditions AlloySelect Select addresses a closely related question: is a material suitable for the specified environment? Users choose the service conditions and candidate material, and the tool provides a screening outcome against the relevant NACE MR0175/ISO 15156 basis, together with applicable notes and restrictions. Those evaluations, where required, remain part of project-specific engineering. A key advantage of AlloySelect CCS is that it will also serve as a central repository for CO₂ stream specifications, industry guidance and technical data generated through Joint Industry Projects (JIPs), bringing together information that engineers can use to support consistent, informed materials decisions. The result helps teams distinguish a potentially acceptable option from one that requires a different selection or additional consideration. That can make early conversations more focused, particularly when project data and design assumptions are still evolving. A screening result is not a substitute for a full specification review, procurement requirements or project-specific qualification. However, it provides an essential starting point, helping engineers identify potential risks early, focus subsequent assessments and make more informed materials decisions. New CCS preview: start with the CO2 stream The new AlloySelect CCS preview extends this engineering-led approach to CO2 transport and storage applications. The demonstrator lets users compare a CO2 stream and its operating conditions against a selected reference specification, review impurity limits and see where the composition warrants closer attention. It also provides rule-based advisories for potential acid-dropout concerns and materials screening. Importantly, these are early warnings rather than a final engineering approval. The CCS preview does not calculate full thermodynamic phase behaviour, acid-dropout quantities or corrosion rates. Those evaluations, where required, remain part of project-specific engineering. A key advantage of AlloySelect CCS is that it will also serve as a central repository for CO₂ stream specifications, industry guidance and technical data generated through Joint Industry Projects (JIPs), bringing together information that engineers can use to support consistent, informed materials decisions. articles.body: Asia Bunkering Europe Gas Shipyards Samsung Heavy teams with Tesser on nuclear-powered LNG carrier Sam Chambers November 19, 2026 0 172 1 minute read South Korea’s Samsung Heavy Industries has entered an exclusive partnership with US reactor developer Tesser Atomics to develop a nuclear-powered LNG carrier, with the companies targeting a demonstration vessel operating commercially between the US and Europe. Under a memorandum of understanding signed on Thursday, Samsung Heavy will serve as the exclusive shipbuilder and Tesser as the exclusive reactor partner for the project, with both companies working on vessel design, reactor integration and regulatory licensing. The project emerged from Norway’s NuProShip research programme and is progressing through SFI SAINT, a maritime research initiative led by the Norwegian University of Science and Technology and supported by the Research Council of Norway. The proposed vessel would use Tesser’s Triton reactor, a compact fluoride-salt-cooled high-temperature system developed specifically for ships. It combines TRISO nuclear fuel with low-pressure molten-salt coolant and is designed to allow refuelling while operating. esser was co-founded by Per Peterson, who also helped establish Kairos Power. While Kairos is focused on land-based electricity generation, Tesser is pursuing marine applications of the technology. Samsung Heavy has been exploring nuclear propulsion and floating nuclear power generation, but the latest tie-up represents a move towards demonstrating the technology on an actual LNG trading route. No shipbuilding contract or firm delivery date has been announced, although the partners are targeting the early 2030s. A Tesser spokesperson told Splash: “The collaboration is designed to move fast, with the first nuclear-powered LNG carrier expected in the early 2030s. articles.body: Americas Offshore Weatherford bags new deepwater drilling deal in Brazil Bojan Lepic November 19, 2026 0 116 1 minute read MarineTraffic / Fabio Roque MarineTraffic / Fabio Roque US oilfield services giant Weatherford has secured a contract from Constellation Oil Services to provide managed pressure drilling (MPD) technology for a deepwater exploration campaign offshore Brazil. The agreement covers Constellation’s ultra-deepwater drillship Amaralina Star and includes an initial 12-month rental of Weatherford’s MPD equipment and technology. It also includes the sale of an MPD system, scheduled for delivery within 12 months, and a two-year aftermarket services contract. Weatherford will support the programme through its Brazilian operations and Managed Pressure Wells Centre of Excellence in Houston. The latest award builds on a separate agreement secured from Constellation in May, covering managed pressure drilling and subsea intervention services offshore Brazil. The 2012-delivered Amaralina Star can operate in water depths of up to 10,000 feet and drill wells to depths of 40,000 feet. Constellation secured a three-year, approximately $528m contract with Petrobras for the drillship in December 2024, covering operations beginning in the first quarter of 2026. That agreement includes work in frontier exploration areas such as Brazil’s Equatorial Margin and Pelotas Basin, with an option for up to 315 additional days. Weatherford chief executive Girish Saligram said the latest contract would strengthen the company’s position in Brazil’s deepwater drilling market while creating opportunities for further equipment and aftermarket services work. Source: NKT via LinkedIn A new cable-lay barge that Danish power cable manufacturer and installation firm NKT purchased from Boskalis last year has been widened by eight meters as part of its transformation into a nearshore cable-laying barge. NKT reported in October 2025 that it had invested in the Boka Constructor cable-lay barge from Dutch Boskalis, with plans to modernize the unit for nearshore cable laying and burial operations. Built in 2016 at Gdynia/Swinemünde, Boka Constructor, now renamed NKT Isabella, is 126 meters long and used to offer accommodation for 50 persons. As part of its transformation program, the barge has been widened by eight meters, increasing its width from 32 to 40 meters, creating space for the cable handling equipment to be installed while helping keep its draft low for operations in ultra-shallow waters. The upgrades have also increased the barge's accommodation capacity to 73 persons. NKT via LinkedIn NKT via LinkedIn Once fully equipped, NKT Isabella will have three cable turntables with a combined capacity of 6,000 tons.
